newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Berlusconi complains over bugging device.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Berlusconi complains over bugging device.

text.p: A lawyer for Italian media mogul Silvio Berlusconi made a formal complaint on Monday about a bugging device found in the former prime minister's office as politicians prepared to debate the affair.

Lawyer Giuseppe De Luca visited police headquarters to deposit two pages of documents containing details of how the bug, whose discovery has caused uproar in Italian politics, was found and Berlusconi's comments on the matter.

"The fact is very serious since, in my role as a parliamentarian, under article 68 of the constitution I cannot be subjected to eavesdropping of any sort without the prior approval of the Chamber of Deputies," Berlusconi wrote.

The leaders of the various parties in the centre-left coalition discussed the affair on Monday with signs of disagreement on whether parliamentary debate should be limited to the bugging or amplified to discuss judicial activities.

Berlusconi, whose global business empire includes a controlling interest in Italy's three main private television stations, told a news conference in Rome on Friday that a sweep of his office had detected the bug on Wednesday.
The centre-right Forza Italia party leader held up the matchbox-sized device for inspection by reporters and said it was in perfect working order with a range of around 300 metres (yards).

The revelation sparked widespread outrage across the parliamentary divide with some centre-right politicians making immediate comparisons to the 1974 Watergate political bugging scandal that toppled U.S. President Richard Nixon.

Disgraced former Socialist prime minister Bettino Craxi declared in a statement issued in Tunisia, where he is a fugitive from Italian justice, that the bugging affair was merely the "latest link in a chain of illegality."
The statement railed at what Craxi saw as an enormous volume of illegal telephone interception with politicians, businessmen, journalists and lawyers all under surveillance.
De Luca said Berlusconi had yet to hand over the microphone, described by some security sources as an amateurish device.
The lawyer said Berlusconi still had "no specific suspicions in any particular direction" about who had planted it.

Referring to the possibility of "deviant offshoots" of official bodies being responsible for the device, De Luca said it was inconceivable to think of "a serious institution violating a principle of democratic law".

Berlusconi has complained repeatedly that he is being victimised by Milan's elite "Clean Hands" pool of anti-corruption magistrates. The media mogul is on trial in Milan for alleged bribes paid by his Fininvest empire to finance police in return for lenient audits. He denies the accusations.
